comparison: Both evaluate the core threat assessment methodology and DD species predictions (C1, C10-C19, C73). OpenEval finds the expert-based approach methodologically sound with appropriate validation. Peer reviewers acknowledge comprehensiveness but express significant concern about 'large uncertainties and embedded biases' in expert opinion, requesting 'statistically supported consideration of the uncertainty.' This represents a fundamental disagreement about confidence in the assessment approach.

Both evaluate threat attribution and overfishing as primary driver (C2, C24-C26). OpenEval finds systematic threat coding provides adequate support. Peer reviewers acknowledge the manuscript 'provides a clear picture of the distributions and patterning of threat,' accepting these threat characterization findings. Strong agreement on this result.

Both evaluate statistical modeling of risk factors including body size, depth, and family-level patterns (C3, C4, C20-C23, C32-C36, C76-C78). OpenEval finds rigorous GLMM analysis with phylogenetic controls. Peer reviewers explicitly praised 'rigorous statistical assessment' and noted this would be 'a valuable scientific contribution.' Strong agreement that statistical modeling results are well-supported.

Both evaluate the lack of range-risk relationship and mechanistic explanations (C37-C40). OpenEval finds statistical demonstration adequate with well-reasoned mechanistic hypotheses. Peer reviewers accepted this as part of the rigorous statistical modeling, distinguishing it as 'strong inferences derived from objective data.' Agreement on this finding.

Both evaluate threat type proportions and habitat-specific patterns (C27-C31). OpenEval finds direct counts from threat coding adequate. Peer reviewers accepted these as part of the distributional assessments 'founded in natural scientific rigor.' Agreement on threat characterization data.

Both evaluate comparative conservation status with other vertebrates (C5, C6, C15, C41-C44). OpenEval finds comparisons appropriate and justified. Peer reviewers raised concerns about potential biases and requested better consideration of uncertainty in expert opinions, noting the comparative claims 'would gain more credibility' with clearer uncertainty quantification. Disagreement on confidence level.

Both evaluate geographic threat patterns and hotspot identification (C7-C9, C67-C72). OpenEval finds systematic spatial analysis with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers acknowledged these distributional assessments as 'highly informative' and 'founded in natural scientific rigor.' Agreement on geographic findings.

Both evaluate comparison with fisheries assessments (C46-C48). OpenEval finds validation against independent data appropriate with conservative interpretation. Peer reviewers specifically questioned this comparison, noting Costello et al. 2012 data suggests 'sharks and rays are better off than the Costello assessment,' raising concerns about potential inconsistency. Disagreement on interpretation of comparative fisheries data.

Both evaluate B/BMSY data and biomass decline calculations (C49, C50, C110). OpenEval accepts these as valid validation data from Costello et al. 2012. Peer reviewers used this same data to question the authors' threat estimates, noting median B/BMSY of 0.37 'is actually worse than the values presented in this paper,' suggesting potential underestimation of threat. Disagreement on how to reconcile these data with expert assessments.

Both evaluate documented population extinctions and regional extirpations (C51-C57). OpenEval finds literature documentation adequate with appropriate uncertainty acknowledgment. Peer reviewers accepted these as factual data points within the objective component. Agreement on extinction documentation.

Both evaluate evolutionary context and life history characteristics (C58-C66). OpenEval finds established knowledge with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers did not challenge these foundational biological claims. Agreement on background biology.

Both evaluate habitat-specific threat patterns and depth effects (C75, C79, C80). OpenEval finds statistical demonstration with mechanistic explanation. Peer reviewers accepted this as part of the rigorous statistical modeling of geographic and life history patterns. Agreement on depth-threat relationships.

Both evaluate DD rate and predictive modeling approach (C16, C17, C74). OpenEval finds methodology sound with good prediction accuracy. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about expert opinion-based assessments extends to confidence in DD predictions, requesting better uncertainty quantification. Disagreement mirrors broader methodological concerns.

Both evaluate IUCN criteria application and assessment process (C81-C83, C92-C93). OpenEval accepts these as factual descriptions with appropriate justification. Peer reviewers acknowledged comprehensiveness but raised concerns about transparency and potential bias in 'adjustments to the data,' questioning reliability despite accepting the methodology description. Disagreement on assessment reliability.

Both evaluate taxonomic discovery trends (C84-C91, C115). OpenEval finds factual documentation adequate. Peer reviewers accepted these as objective taxonomic data. Agreement on species discovery patterns.

Both evaluate conservation policy effectiveness and international protections (C94-C102). OpenEval finds documentation adequate with reasonable inferences. Peer reviewers explicitly criticized these as 'anecdotal and potentially biased,' noting 'only a subset of the legislation specific to the taxon is reported' and suggesting removal from Results. Strong disagreement on scientific rigor of policy assessments.

Both evaluate fisheries data quality issues (C103-C108, C116). OpenEval finds factual observations about reporting limitations. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these characterizations as context for data limitations. Agreement on data quality problems.

Both evaluate assessment methodology scale and expert participation (C92-C93). OpenEval finds multi-workshop approach with broad participation supports credibility. Peer reviewers acknowledged this as comprehensive but questioned 'how much stock we can put into even the opinions of the world's experts.' Disagreement on whether scale ensures reliability.

Both evaluate freshwater threat patterns (C28, C45). OpenEval finds consistency with broader freshwater biodiversity patterns strengthens findings. Peer reviewers accepted threat characterization data. Agreement on freshwater threats.

Both evaluate Blue shark life history parameters (C112-C114). OpenEval finds cited parameters relevant to assessment challenges. Peer reviewers accepted these as literature-based data points. Agreement on species-specific examples.

Both evaluate Mediterranean validation studies (C109, C111). OpenEval finds independent quantitative validation supports expert assessments. Peer reviewers accepted these as objective validation data from cited studies. Agreement on validation evidence.
